paragraphs.heading: A bigger cousin of the asteroid belt
paragraphs.text: The Kuiper belt is a disc of small bodies in the outer Solar System. It starts at Neptune's orbit, 30 astronomical units (AU) from the Sun, and runs out to about 50 AU. It resembles the asteroid belt but is far bigger: 20 times as wide and 20 to 200 times as massive. Like the asteroid belt, it is mostly leftovers from when the Solar System formed. But where many asteroids are mainly rock and metal, most Kuiper belt objects are largely frozen volatiles, called ices, such as methane, ammonia and water.

paragraphs.heading: Home of the dwarf planets
paragraphs.text: Most of the bodies that astronomers generally accept as dwarf planets live here: Orcus, Pluto, Haumea, Quaoar and Makemake. Of all its known members, Pluto is both the biggest and the heaviest. Its orbit marks it as one of the plutinos, a class of Kuiper belt objects that share the same 2:3 resonance with Neptune. A few moons now circling other worlds may also have begun here, among them Triton, which orbits Neptune, and Phoebe, which orbits Saturn.

paragraphs.heading: Its neighbours
paragraphs.text: The belt was first thought to be the main source of periodic comets, those that come round in less than 200 years. Studies since the mid-1990s show instead that the belt is stable, and that those comets really come from the scattered disc. That is a restless zone made when Neptune moved outward 4.5 billion years ago, and its members, such as Eris, follow very stretched orbits reaching as far as 100 AU. Farther still lies the proposed Oort cloud, thought to be a thousand times more distant and mostly ball-shaped. Together, all these far-off bodies are called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs).

paragraphs.heading: Guesses before the evidence
paragraphs.text: After Pluto was found in 1930, many wondered whether it was alone. Soon after, the astronomer Frederick C. Leonard asked whether Pluto might be the first of a series of bodies beyond Neptune still waiting to be found. In 1943 Kenneth Edgeworth argued that past Neptune the early material was too spread out to build planets, so it formed countless smaller bodies instead, and that one would sometimes wander inward as a comet. In 1951 Gerard Kuiper suggested a similar disc, and the belt now carries his name.

paragraphs.heading: Kuiper's wrong turn
paragraphs.text: Kuiper himself did not expect the belt to still be there. He believed Pluto had swept through the zone from 30 to 50 AU and scattered its comets across the Solar System. Like others of his time, he assumed Pluto was much more massive than we now know it is. Had he been right, there would be no Kuiper belt today.

paragraphs.heading: Clues and the first find
paragraphs.text: In 1980 Julio Ángel Fernández made the most direct prediction, a comet belt beyond Neptune feeding short-period comets. Another clue came from the centaurs, comet-like bodies between Jupiter and Neptune. Their orbits only last a few million years, so ever since Chiron was found in 1977, astronomers have reasoned that some outer store must keep refilling them. Direct proof finally came in 1992, with the discovery of 15760 Albion, the first such object found since Pluto and Charon. Thousands are now known, and more than 100000 wider than 100 km are thought to exist.
